body:
@paul-gauthier Sorry for the oversight & appreciate the feedback! I didn't realize there's a specific blog directly discussing the "repo-map" - we will be sure to cite and discuss them in the next revision of the preprint :) (cc @czlll)

I have to admit, even though we are discussing this under the thread of Aider-inspired RepoMap, the question we were trying to answer in this paper is more about which is better, "agentic-based information gathering" or "passively provided information" (e.g., via embedding, where the LLM has few options to control the information being retrieved). IRRC, the original AiderMap is designed primarily for the latter category, and it didn't immediately jump into my mind when reviewing the paper 😅 .

But now, reflecting back, the indexing approach we took does look similar to what AiderMap was doing under the hood and we will certainly discuss it and give credits.

I'd say the differences between LocAgent vs. Aider are more about "how LLMs are using these graph-based indexing." My (maybe outdated) knowledge of Aider is that it automatically constructs a RepoMap for LLM (based on previously mentioned keywords, etc) to provide the context for LLM to perform edit (more similar to the passively provided information); whereas LocAgent is more about allowing LLM to use tools to explicitly traverse the graph (more leaning towards agentic-based information gathering - which is something we are hoping to continue to do in OpenHands).

author: tobitege

body:
Yes, you could add the command to remove the Poetry cache in the Makefile as a preventative measure. However, it might be considered too aggressive to delete the cache every time make build is run, as this could slow down the build process and remove potentially useful cached files. It is generally better to handle cache issues as they arise rather than preemptively clearing the cache every time.

Here's why I suggest not adding this to the Makefile:

1. Performance Impact: Deleting the cache can lead to longer build times as dependencies will need to be re-fetched and re-installed from scratch.
2. Unnecessary Deletion: In many cases, the cache does not cause issues and deleting it every time would be redundant.
3. Cache Benefits: The cache can speed up subsequent builds by reusing previously downloaded and compiled packages.

Instead, consider clearing the cache manually or as part of a specific troubleshooting process when you encounter related issues.

Is there a way for a prompt to include information the contents of a file, or specifically, to include the contents of the `.gitignore`?

After experimenting with the system prompt, I found that if I explicitly listed the files to ignore (eg. "ignore the `main.py` and `index.py` files as they are in the `.gitignore`", the agent would consistently ignore them. However, instructions for the agent to first read the `.gitignore` and then ignore all files listed there was unsuccessful.

Specifically, adding this to the `minimal_system_prompt` did not work:

```
When issuing any commands or viewing any files or folders, first make sure these files are not in the .gitignore, and if they are in the .gitignore please ignore them.

So your first step should be to see if there is a .gitignore file, and if there is a .gitignore file read the file so that you know what files to ignore.

If you believe any action should be taken with a file or folder in the .gitignore file or you should search these files, instead indicate you are skipping them because they are in the .gitignore file.
```

But if I specified the file names it was fine, and had a nice UX of saying when it found a match but was ignoring it. So I am looking for a way to read this content into a prompt. Can someone point me in the right direction? I couldn't find a similar example of incorporating workspace info in the prompt.

For the curious, here are some other things I tried but did not work:

- Telling the system prompt to ignore contents of .gitignore, then separately, as a user asking opendevin to read the .gitignore. It read the contents, but kept answering questions about the .gitignore listed files.
- Then as a user, sent another reminder to ignore contents of the .gitignore. This didn't work.

Because of these experiments, I don't think sending OpenDevin a sequence of messages through code would work (like read the .gitignore, and then ignore those files). It seems like the files need to be explicitly listed.

- I experimented with updating the `search_dir(search_term, dir_path='./')` skill so that it took an `exclude_files` argument. This sometimes worked, but other times, it would use the `/api/list-files` to find the file.

body:
> If the last line of the observation is `SyntaxError: invalid syntax` for 5 times in a row... somethings _really_ wrong. 😄

Yeah! Part of the problem is we don't detect this as an error observation. It's just an observation. There is code in is_stuck() detecting if the agent encountered an error for doing the same action over and over, even if the error isn't the same. We stop that. But this isn't recognized as an error. (and the reason here is that is_stuck code was mostly following the patterns of behavior of monologue agent, which did result in errors recognized as errors)

Maybe we should just recognize this case exactly as you suggest. We can add that it's an IPythonRunCellObservation and the action is the same. We will have the same bit with the action (it won't be the same when it uses 'mistakes' or 'errors'), but it should stop sooner than it does now.

body:
The agents are here:
https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/tree/main/agenthub

There is a README on the folder, though I don't think it answers your question, it's more geared for agent research and development, which is their purpose.

The best suggestion I can give is actually to use CodeAct unless you have a reason to use another. CodeAct, SWE-CodeAct and Monologue are generic agents, with the other two older and not as good. Others are in development, micro-agents or delegates are experimental and might be used by other agents as necessary (by CodeAct perhaps, in the future). Browsing agent is fine, but as the name says, it's specialized and its main use will probably be via another, for browsing tasks.

body:
Apologies, I did not correctly understand. So I asked for help: 😁 

Let's break down each of the commands:

1. **`pushd evaluation/swe_bench`**:
   - This command changes the current directory to `evaluation/swe_bench` and saves the current directory on the directory stack. The `pushd` command is useful for navigating directories while keeping track of where you came from. You can return to the original directory with the `popd` command.

2. **`docker build -t ghcr.io/opendevin/eval-swe-bench:full-v1.2.1 -f ./scripts/docker/Dockerfile.full.v1.1 .`**:
   - This command builds a Docker image using the Dockerfile located at `./scripts/docker/Dockerfile.full.v1.1`.
   - The `-t` flag tags the resulting image with the name `ghcr.io/opendevin/eval-swe-bench:full-v1.2.1`.
   - The `.` at the end specifies the build context, which is the current directory (`evaluation/swe_bench`).

3. **`docker push ghcr.io/opendevin/eval-swe-bench:full-v1.2.1`**:
   - This command pushes the Docker image `ghcr.io/opendevin/eval-swe-bench:full-v1.2.1` to the GitHub Container Registry.
   - This makes the image available for others to pull and use from the GitHub Container Registry.

In summary, these commands change to the `evaluation/swe_bench` directory, build a Docker image from a specified Dockerfile, and then push the resulting image to the GitHub Container Registry.`

body:
> Well if it's going through the headers 1-by-1 and diagramming them, and since the header itself appears in the log I posted, I guess my question becomes:
> 
> **Do you really think that header above in the log is 5,000,000 chars long?**
> 
> EDIT: This might explain how I spent $20 last night on the API diagramming headers...

max_chars keeps count of all calls to the API during a session, not just one message. So if this is step 42, it includes a count of characters in the other steps too and their history. In other words, it counts your successive contexts sent to the openai API. Also, at least in some cases, I think it also includes stuff done before, e.g. when you are asked if you want to resume the same session and successfully do so (it's using the same session and continues to count), but I should say it's not clear to me this last one was the case here or not.

The intention of this `max_chars` variable check is precisely to allow users to control cost in some way. It might not be a perfect way... it's one way.

We actually have a newer feature more on point, I think, `max_budget_per_task`. New enough to me too that I haven't actually tried it yet. 😅 Its meaning is exactly what you'd think: the maximum budget (in USD) allowed per task, beyond which the agent will stop.

body:
You can set llm parameters, including `temperature` and `max_output_tokens`, in config.toml. Something like this works:
```
...
[gpt-name-it-as-you-like]
model="GPT-4o"
api_key=...
temperature=0
max_output_tokens=4096
...
[claude]
model="Claude-opus..."
api_key=...
temperature=0
max_output_tokens=2048
...
```
The section names here are user-defined. Then when running main.py, use the respective section name with -l or --llm-config, e.g. `main.py --llm-config=claude ...`

Note that all attributes of LLMConfig class from opendevin.core.config.py can be set in custom llm configs this way, but the agents are able to override them. Currently most agents don't override anything as far as I know, except CodeAct and CodeActSWE on temperature: they always call the API with `temperature=0`.

body:
Here is my design concept after a very brief look at the existing code. Let me know if you have any concerns.

I will add two agents:
1. ```VantagePointAgent``` (head agent; based on CodeAct)
2. ```OmniscientChatBot``` (sub-agent; based on ClaudeCLI repo)

The reason why I intend to make a new head agent (instead of modifying ```CodeActAgent```) is:
Not all providers have a model appropriate for ```OmniscientChatBot```.
Not all users will have an API key for Anthropic.
Thus it is better to leave the default head agent as-is (presently CodeAct?) and provide ```VantagePointAgent``` for those who do have an API key for Anthropic.

One of my assumptions is that it might be tricky to add and remove capabilities dynamically because they depend on the example chat string that we use to teach the model how to use those capabilities. (multi-shot prompting) That's one reason why I will make a new head agent.

I intend to do this in two stages:
1. Initial implementation will support a single API key (Anthropic) for both agents, so that I don't need to change the UI for inputting API keys. OmniscientChatBot will be stateless, without access to a conversation history. Will submit a working version with these limitations.
2. Second stage will support two API keys, so that the VantagePointAgent can use for example GPT-4o and the OmniscientChatBot can be either Gemini 1.5 Flash or Claude Haiku.

> Detect if it is actual code then use a monospace font, otherwise a "regular" font

There is a `<SyntaxHighlighter>` component that handles styling code blocks:
https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/c6951eb6c1bbf1d03f8023470b053d5146f6a2f1/frontend/src/components/markdown/code.tsx#L23-L31

To address your other points:

Actually the chat bubbles are already able to render markdown with the `<Markdown>` component here:
https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/c6951eb6c1bbf1d03f8023470b053d5146f6a2f1/frontend/src/components/chat/ChatMessage.tsx#L19-L23

What happens in your screenshot is that LLM responds with markdown as a language ID for the syntax highlighter rather than actual markdown. The component then moves it into the classname and is handled by the `code` component

The raw text that the LLM in the screenshot generated is actually something like:
\`\`\`markdown
\# Title
\#\# Subtitle
\`\`\`

Where 'markdown' is the language ID that is moved to the classname to be handled by the custom `code` component.

Because of the backticks, they end up being wrapped in `<code>` elements, which remove any markdown styling provided by the `<Markdown>` component.

Trying to change the current logic to support rendering proper markdown in code blocks, may not be so straightforward due to how the `<Markdown>` and `<SyntaxHighligher>` components work under the hood, though I believe it is possible.

Another alternative I could think of is to update the prompt to specify the LLM not to wrap markdown text in a code block unless directly specified to do so.

---

body:
### Here's Gemini's suggestion (this is the unit tests one. Edit: below is "as is", I didn't review the changes):

The issue stems from GitHub Actions marking a job as failed when it encounters a running CodeCov upload. Since the CodeCov upload often occurs while tests are still running, this leads to the "red cross" even though the tests might still be in progress.

To resolve this, you can leverage the `fail_ci_if_error` option provided by the `codecov/codecov-action@v4`. By setting it to `false`, CodeCov will not mark the job as failed if an error occurs during the upload process, allowing the tests to complete and determine the final status of the job.

Here's the improved GitHub Actions workflow:

```yaml
name: Run Unit Tests

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths-ignore:
      - '**/*.md'
      - 'frontend/**'
      - 'docs/**'
      - 'evaluation/**'
  pull_request:

env:
  PERSIST_SANDBOX : "false"

jobs:
  test-on-macos:
    name: Test on macOS
    runs-on: macos-13
    env:
      INSTALL_DOCKER: "1" # Set to '0' to skip Docker installation
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11"]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install poetry via pipx
        run: pipx install poetry

      - name: Set up Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: "poetry"

      - name: Install Python dependencies using Poetry
        run: poetry install

      - name: Install & Start Docker
        if: env.INSTALL_DOCKER == '1'
        run: |
          brew install colima docker
          colima start

          # For testcontainers to find the Colima socket
          # https://github.com/abiosoft/colima/blob/main/docs/FAQ.md#cannot-connect-to-the-docker-daemon-at-unixvarrundockersock-is-the-docker-daemon-running
          sudo ln -sf $HOME/.colima/default/docker.sock /var/run/docker.sock

      - name: Build Environment
        run: make build

      - name: Run Tests
        run: poetry run pytest --forked --cov=agenthub --cov=opendevin --cov-report=xml ./tests/unit -k "not test_sandbox"

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          fail_ci_if_error: false # This line has been added
        env:
          CODECOV_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
  test-on-linux:
    name: Test on Linux
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      INSTALL_DOCKER: "0" # Set to '0' to skip Docker installation
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11"]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install poetry via pipx
        run: pipx install poetry

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: "poetry"

      - name: Install Python dependencies using Poetry
        run: poetry install --without evaluation

      - name: Build Environment
        run: make build

      - name: Run Tests
        run: poetry run pytest --forked --cov=agenthub --cov=opendevin --cov-report=xml ./tests/unit -k "not test_sandbox"

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          fail_ci_if_error: false # This line has been added
        env:
          CODECOV_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}

  test-for-sandbox:
    name: Test for Sandbox
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install poetry via pipx
        run: pipx install poetry

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: "poetry"

      - name: Install Python dependencies using Poetry
        run: poetry install

      - name: Build Environment
        run: make build

      - name: Run Integration Test for Sandbox
        run: |
          poetry run pytest --cov=agenthub --cov=opendevin --cov-report=xml -s ./tests/unit/test_sandbox.py

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          fail_ci_if_error: false # This line has been added
        env:
          CODECOV_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
```

By adding `fail_ci_if_error: false` within the `with` block of each `codecov/codecov-action@v4` step, the CodeCov upload will no longer prematurely mark the job as failed, allowing the "yellow spinner" to appear correctly while the tests are running.

body:
The design is great.

If I understand you correctly, the `od-runtime-client` will install all needed packages/plugins to the target sandbox to smoothly execute all tasks received from the OD server through the WebSocket connection. 

I have a few worries about the dependencies, package installation, and plugin management. 

> we might also consider merging all the existing plugins into `od-runtime-client`

Will the `od-runtime-client` grow significantly over time, or does it only consist of basic plugins and it can pull others from the remote?

BTW, how do we define the plugins? Is it possible to let the users define their own plugins?
author: iFurySt

body:
> Will the od-runtime-client grow significantly over time, or does it only consist of basic plugins and it can pull others from the remote?

This is a very good question! For simplicity now, we can just say we want to pack everything at the beginning (maybe keep the "setup.sh" based workflow for our plugins now).

> BTW, how do we define the plugins? Is it possible to let the users define their own plugins?

Now user can already define their own plugins via `setup.sh`.

But in the long term, we should consider make this plugin management very easy, so that user can easily define their plugins. I have a preliminary thought about using a Python package manager like `pip` for plugin management -- user can bring their own pip package to the system, and we basically need a `pip install` to install it.

Besides this, I'm also debating the difference between `plugins` and `agentskills`:

- I view plugins more like a heavy OD-specific dependency that is required to support certain things (e.g., if we have a VSCode frontend, we may have a `vscode` plugin that needs to be activated inside `od-runtime-client` so it can directly take to vscode for code editing actions). This should/can be transparent to the end user that just want to use OD to solve tasks.

- `agentskills` is more like a custom library of tools that user can easily add new capabilities into it, whether it is for support new modality (e.g., `transcribe_speech_to_text`) or customized workflow (e.g., `lookup_my_calendar`). User should be aware of this, and can new actions to it when needed. I'm thinking maybe we should focus more on lowering the entry barrier for user here?

I mostly replicated the issue described by @mamoodi, using `main` branch, on Mac, building with `make build / make run` as in the post. Except for the UI part. I mean, there are two things here, aside from the toml:

body:
@tobitege The original question is how to obtain the session's full trajectory data in order to obtain a larger dataset of which we can do better analysis that is harder to achieve with a session's partial trajectory data.

One solution is to send the session's full trajectory data automatically and anonymously to the backend before the user ended their session (whether by disconnecting or closing), but as you can tell may not be so privacy-friendly at this stage, and the user may not be so happy.

It is already unlikely the user themselves will press the stop action in order to display the feedback dialog (in whichever format). Do you think there is a better chance the user will share full data at the end of the session if they are prompted to do so at the beginning?

Can you by any chance think of any other alternatives?
author: amanape

body:
I definitely understand that this issue is between a hard stone and a rock.
First, though, there needs to be some user opt-out or opt-in option for sending any data, like all the cookie confirmation prompts, but more decisive, especially with regard to e.g. EU privacy laws. I know that these exist but not all the details to them.
Just being on the "safe side" to avoid potential trouble from the get-go.

The desire to collect data I can understand, but personally I'd by default would not want it enabled unless being asked.
So that leads me to: whenever the UI pops up, check if the user has been previously asked and consented or not. Remember the user's choice and obey it.
Add an option to the Settings modal in case the user changes their mind.
If they voluntarily click the up-/down-buttons, then good, but do not take
that as a permanent consent statement.

Does that make sense?
author: tobitege

body:
@tobitege The implementation was never going to send data without the users knowledge. It would only be sent after the user explicitly does so.

You do make a point though.

CC @neubig
After some review, GDPR requires us to ask the user for consent to share data through a privacy notice. E.g.,
"We collect chat logs to improve our service. Your data will be handled in accordance with our privacy policy. Do you agree to proceed? [Yes] [No]"

Something of the sorts must be displayed to the user when pressing either action button. Though we can display the same exact notice every time the user presses the button to submit feedback (if they previously declined).

It is absolutely required to do so if we are send personal data / PII with the feedback as well, which we do with their email and name (it may also be the case that the user shares certain PII during the chat, which could also fall under the same requirement)

To clarify: we must state the exact nature on how the data their sharing is being used (to train a model, update our service, etc...) to allow the user to decide whether they want to opt in or out, especially in cases where we receive their personal data as well.

author: tobitege

body:
Just as one possible scenario: a parent lets their non-adult kid use OpenDevin and might not supervise every step.
There is no way for the parent to a) disable any feedback and b) prevent the use of their email if its already pre-filled.
Above might actually raise another issue or two by itself, but that's my thinking about it.
author: tobitege

body:
Setting up an auth provider is way too much work (verify email, set password, change password, GDPR delete account, request info, etc...) for little value right now.

> Just as one possible scenario: a parent lets their kid use OpenDevin and might not supervise every step.
There is no way for the parent to a) disable any feedback and b) prevent the use of their email if its alread pre-filled.
Above might actually raise another issue or two by itself, but that's my thinking about it.

Actually, now that I think of it, I'm not sure if requiring the user to share their email is entirely necessary. Maybe we can do without it for now and send it anonymized until we see a more solid requirements for it (e.g., responding to the user that shared the feedback for some reason)

From [here](https://opendevin.github.io/OpenDevin/modules/usage/llms/localLLMs#select-your-model)

>In the OpenDevin UI, click on the Settings wheel in the bottom-left corner. Then in the Model input, enter ollama/codellama:7b, or the name of the model you pulled earlier. If it doesn’t show up in a dropdown, that’s fine, just type it in. Click Save when you’re done.

I don't think this issue need to be worried about. Currently, we rely on `litellm` to acquire full list of models, it may be slow to include all the models in the market.

```python
@app.get('/api/options/models')
async def get_litellm_models():
    """
    Get all models supported by LiteLLM.

    To get the models:
    ```sh
    curl http://localhost:3000/api/litellm-models
    ```
    """
    litellm_model_list = litellm.model_list + list(litellm.model_cost.keys())
    litellm_model_list_without_bedrock = bedrock.remove_error_modelId(
        litellm_model_list
    )
    bedrock_model_list = bedrock.list_foundation_models()
    model_list = litellm_model_list_without_bedrock + bedrock_model_list

    return list(sorted(set(model_list)))
```

body:
> After Devin completes a task, I often manually adjust the results. [...]

That is an interesting idea, for which I might have a possible first iteration ready (waiting for one PR to make it through, to build on it).
Idea is like you said: have an observer help to check if a file that is _about_ to be opened or edited, has changed since last time. 
In that case, I'd output a message to the LLM that the operation is not performed and it shall decide to repeat the request and/or re-view the file.
After that, the file gets removed from being marked as "changed" and the LLM could then fire the edit command again and it would go through.

How does that sound (even if a bit techy 😁 )?

2. Cline - enterprise focus, open, and thoughtful product management. No IntelliJ support right now, but it is being considered
3. Continue.dev - had issues compiling. Has IntelliJ support as well. It is less popular (stars and forks) than Cline
4. VoidEditor - a fork of VS Code. With VS Code cracking down on the forks and limited upside, making it less desirable

I plan to base my initial efforts on Cline as a fork for OpenHands as seemingly. I hope Cline could become a dependency instead of a fork to reduce maintenance efforts but that will be a different workstream for me.

Could someone in Open Hands product management role give feedback on the approach and the choice? I want to get some validation before spending much time on Cline.

body:
For the record, [slack discussion](https://openhands-ai.slack.com/archives/C07V9BMGHH6/p1745847596901669).

I think maybe we can look at this in multiple ways. Here is just one, please take it as just some brainstorming fodder, and feel free to shred to pieces if it seems inaccurate or doesn't fit what you'd like:

The first important question, it seems to me, is whether a vscode extension is _an alternative frontend_ to OpenHands, or not.

I think the answer here should be yes: I imagine a tab where the user can enter a message, the extension communicates via socket.io with the openhands server, sends the task, gets the results, displays them.[1]

#### Note: OpenHands 100-feet view
- backend -> communicates via socket.io server -> frontend, by default a web UI

#### Example: Plan/Act

Allow me to take the Plan/Act mode as an example of seemingly more advanced functionality.

OpenHands actually has the backend for that:
- we recently merged a readonly codeact agent, a version of the agent that the user can use to explore the code and - if they want - plan; it has tools to read, not to "act"
- both agents, the default codeact and the readonly one, can have different LLMs set by the user
- so when an agent is running, it will run it with its own LLM.

OpenHands doesn't have a visual interface that makes use of this functionality.

Maybe, if you think plan/act is great UX, we could take this flow and display it in a vscode tab, name it simply and clearly as plan/act modes?

To note, for it to work, we would need the appropriate API routes, to send / receive this information. The current web API server is very tightly coupled to the current web UI frontend, which is limited - it's disconnected from these backend functionalities. So I imagine we would add API endpoints like set/get the plan/act modes options, and set/get current mode.

For the extension, this is just an example of functionality in addition to or on top of the basic vscode tab. I guess such tab would include the chat-like components that are usual for user/agent communication.

---

[1] If there are reasons for the answer to be 'no', then it would seem very important to me to point them out. I do think this question is essential and shapes the rest of the discussion/issues/workflow here.

body:
So it sounds like there are a couple separable desires here:

* For this issue, I think we should focus on making VS Code a window into the current OpenHands functionality. 
* Second, there is probably new functionality (e.g. plan/act) that we want to have, which might make even more sense once we have an IDE extension

Focusing on #1, some open questions:
* At minimum I think we need a chat window, which will kick off a new OH conversation
  * Does it have to connect to a running OH server? Or does it start up OH on the fly?
  * Does it run commands in a container, or do we use LocalRuntime to use your local machine?
  * Does it edit files locally, or does it clone the repo and pass its changes through a remote branch on eg GitHub?
     * probably local
* Can a VS Code user see OH working inside of VS Code? E.g. can they see the edited files?
  * This seems like must-have
  * We could potentially use SSH mode to connect into the OpenHands runtime container
  * Or if OH is working on local files, that's easy
* Stretch: can we register the local VS Code as a "remote runtime"?
  * it could connect to the websocket, listen for e.g. CmdRunAction, run it in the terminal, then send back a CmdOutputObservation
  * ditto for file ops
  * we're not 100% set up to do this but it wouldn't be super hard, and it's always been a goal of mine

body:
Update! We now have 3 parts to tackle this functionality.

**1) CLI-VSCode Integration**  
Like the original post's request:
> VSCode extension that allows users to interact with OpenDevin directly within the editor. Users should be able to:
> - Select code snippets directly in draft popup to send to OpenDevin.
> - Right-click on a file and send it as part of a prompt request.

This is less than a full OH extension (which has its own UI and flow). It auto-installs when the user starts `openhands` in a VSCode terminal, then can send snippets or files to OH.

PR here, thoughts appreciated:
- https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/pull/9085

**2) UI Extension**  
This is the extension mentioned above. I'll admit, I didn't see clearly all the implications clearly from the start. It began with a chat tab showing OH events as they happen. Displaying user prompts, file views, and edits seemed straightforward. Then I got to command execution (CmdRunAction/obs), and things got... interesting.

My thinking was: if we're showing commands in VSCode, we need to:
- Create an 'OpenHands' terminal
- Execute commands there
- Show the observation
- Send it back to the tab and OH

But that's not how it worked - the OH server executes everything in the background and sends "echoes" to the tab. If the extension created a terminal and sent commands there, it would be *just display*, not actual execution. That didn't sound right to me. If we have a VSCode OH terminal, shouldn't it actually *execute things?*

So it seems we need a VSCode runtime.

**3) VSCode Runtime**  
This PR takes a stab at it:
- https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/pull/9064

I think this is what Robert meant here:
> Stretch: can we register the local VS Code as a "remote runtime"?
> - it could connect to the websocket, listen for e.g. CmdRunAction, run it in the terminal, then send back a CmdOutputObservation
> - ditto for file ops

But I don't think it's a stretch - it's necessary if we want a terminal that actually executes commands, in an OH dedicated terminal "split" from OH server.

**Current Understanding:**
- CLI integration works standalone (no runtime needed)
- UI extension is fully local, and should work on `workspaceFolders`
- Some file ops already work in VSCode workspace folders
- Runtime passes through actual command execution in VSCode environment
- Bonus possibility: bidirectional edits (user + agent modifications synced)

Am I missing something here? Happy to adjust course if my assumptions are off.

body:
Currently, there is a problem with the LLM's context window. Models with small context windows stand no chance against models with 128k+ window. There is already a short & long-term memory system integrated. However, i don't think that memory is encoded and discipte the current memory structure context window is still an issue. I did see an attempt to add a separate memgpt-agent as discussed on #530. It would be great if the memgpt features can be integrated into all the agents so the context window of an llm becomes irrelevant. 


Theoretically, output generated by a 4k window model can also be stored in the short-term memory, so when the model continues to generate response after reaching max token, it can successfully pickup where it left off without getting lost.

https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/docs/ecosystem/memgpt/

@xingyaoww i know there is already a PR open with over a month long contribution for better memory management. However, memgpt is an overall better implementation for the following reasons:

1- If I'm correct, #2021 only targets codeactagent, but memgpt can be used as the default memory for all the agents, which will improve overall quality from planning to execution. 
2- Currently #2021 is testing with a 32k context window, but the memgpt can allow even the 4k and 8k window models to be as capable as 128k window models. body:
This is a very good point. One thing we were trying was to keep user messages for longer time, to make sure we don't lose the task with whatever the user may have specified. That was rather rough, and it doesn't concern agent messages.

Current implementation has a `condensable` flag on messages, that would in theory allow us to make a decision to keep some, but it doesn't atm choose to keep any other than the system message and something like it.

I've done some work on prompts that would make the LLM, during summarization, choose in a more appropriate manner, that is, considering the importance to some messages in function of both time and contents, but it wasn't systematic, not clearly better, and anyway it was for the old agent (not CodeAct). Maybe you're right that it would work better to separate the two: have an LLM make a pass and assign weights, then perform the summarization. Or maybe a better step-by-step prompt.

I think currently we just need to make sure that the summaries are detailed enough that they do keep information, such that the agent is guided forward helpfully. I am yet to test @khushvind 's prompts on the SWE-bench tasks, but I'll get to do that. If you wish to try it, it's PR #2937

body:
> I've done some work on prompts that would make the LLM, during summarization, choose in a more appropriate manner, that is, considering the importance to some messages in function of both time and contents, but it wasn't systematic, not clearly better, and anyway it was for the old agent (not CodeAct). Maybe you're right that it would work better to separate the two: have an LLM make a pass and assign weights, then perform the summarization. Or maybe a better step-by-step prompt.


If we could have a separate 'memory-monitor-agent' that analyze the current event steam and messages (maybe both the user input and system messages if that includes new important findings regarding the user message) before summarized then highlights and stores the key contexts in a parallel priority-stream ( a separate event stream of priotize message); the priority-stream then could be used as a guard rail alongside the the event-steam to guide the agents. In this case, agents will access 2 memories, 1(event stream/current memory) for task completion, and 2(priority stream) to validate the task accuracy and appropriateness. 

Having multiple steams of messages can work better with a long context base workload. Each memory stream will perform different purposes like being used to validate the outcome and regular CoT. This way, if the current memory stream loses or overlooks some crucial context, the separate memory stream can inject that back into the workflow. 

There could also be another memory stream that stores the routes or options to avoid or the faulty approach. This can potentially prevent loops. However, this may require some additional safe guarding to avoid storing valid approaches and preventing complications.

Main issue with single memory stream:
- Contains all the memories in one place. It's good for CoT but has a risk of exceeding context window. With summarization, key context can be lost or less emphasized.

Solution:
- Multiple memory stream with dedicated purpose can overcome the issue of losing key contexts by storing them separately. These additional memory streams can be used through recall to recalibrate the agent's action. Since these additional steams will store only limited memories, it will be much smaller compared to the main memory stream and can be included in the context window for additional arguments.

I don't think this was the blog I was looking for; but it's also about memory management:

contextual embedding may be able to capture more than regular word embedding but it still poses the risk of missing the subtle nuances. 

LLM is instruct-tuned to better understand natural language and its subtleness. Summarizing using AI's capabilities to understand language will capture the meaning closest to the original text. after summarization, it can be contextually embedded which still requires testing with or without embedding.

body:
RE: https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/issues/2487#issuecomment-2254833846

> this describes a vector database where texts are converted into numbers and stored in a relational high-dimensional space.

@rezzie-rich That's not what the 'Sparse Priming Representation' stuff is about. It's more about abstracting/summarizing the key points from the supplied text, while removing any 'irrelevant boilerplate' / wasted tokens / etc. You can see the methodology in the prompts:

- https://github.com/daveshap/SparsePrimingRepresentations#spr-generator
- https://github.com/daveshap/SparsePrimingRepresentations#spr-decompressor

Obviously that may still not be useful/relevant here, but I want to make sure we're at least not discounting it based on false assumptions.

This specific issue seems more like a replacement for MoE for llm architecture. However, this can be replicated using an agent framework. 

The workflow could be like:

User prompt -> extracter-agent(extracting the objective) -> generator-agent(generating the first draft) -> reviewer-agent (reviews the draft and highlights the key areas) -> rag-agent (retrieves relevant info) -> verifier-agent (verifies reviewer-agents output with rag-agents findings) -> generator-agent (generates the final output)


Using multiple task specific llms, as mentioned in #2075 and #486, can get a cheaper and better output than just using gpt-4o for all of them.

Echoing discussion from https://opendevin.slack.com/archives/C078L0FUGUX/p1719450369932329?thread_ts=1718893390.852169&cid=C078L0FUGUX here:

`truncate_observation` truncate each single observation so that it is not too big. I remember i ran some early swe-bench experiments and decided the 99% (or 95%) percentile of the observation is around 10k, and set the truncation default to that (it shouldn't interfere too much with eval - but ofc it will be good to test!). In some cases, if we don't set the limit, some pip install log will gets too long that it will just blow off the context window directly...

EDIT: Check the swe-bench visualizer on HF space (https://huggingface.co/spaces/OpenDevin/evaluation?filepaths=outputs%2Fswe_bench_lite%2FCodeActAgent%2Fgpt-4o-2024-05-13_maxiter_30_N_v1.6-no-hint%2Foutput.jsonl) and open a random swe-bench experiment run. You can find the statistics of observation size: 10k is more like 90-95% percentile. Increasing it might bring some performance benefit, but we can't say for sure until we run the experiment.

_IF_ neither the user nor OpenDevin can predict if/when any action would trigger a safety threshold, it makes it quite hard to judge what makes the effort worthwhile.

Personally, I've run Gemini with different sites/providers and not once got my input related to coding blocked. In that vein, I'd prefer it as an opt-in option for the user, i.e. via the usual config values (toml and/or LITELLM_ env vars etc.), along with appropriate documentation.
But for safety concerns not as a default "unlock" as not only adults could use OpenDevin.

body:
@tobitege 
Thank you for your insights and clarifications. I appreciate the practical perspective on the current state of agent capabilities.

I wanted to share that there has been significant academic discussion around the use of multi-agent systems for task decomposition and mutual verification to enhance output quality. These approaches have shown potential in improving the quality of work by leveraging the strengths of multiple agents in a collaborative manner.

Currently, it seems that OpenDevin’s primary focus is still largely on single-agent systems( mainly in codeact agent). The existing Delegate agent mechanism for multi-agent coordination appears to have seen limited advancements. Additionally, the micro agents being orchestrated seem to be overly simplistic, and the overall effectiveness of multi-agent chaining in practical scenarios is not very impressive.

What I hope to see in a more sophisticated system is a framework with multiple specialized agents, such as:

A planning agent that can decompose tasks and update them based on actual outputs.
An agent specifically for understanding repository contents.
A coding agent to handle the coding tasks.
A testing agent to manage test cases.
A review agent to oversee code quality and perform code reviews.
These agents would work collaboratively, sharing critical information and thereby ensuring a higher quality of output. Such a system would leverage the strengths of different agents working in tandem to efficiently and effectively complete complex tasks.

Looking forward to further discussions on how we can potentially incorporate these ideas into OpenDevin.

body:
To address the issue of the `eval-num-workers` setting being hard-coded and inconsistent across evaluation benchmarks, you can add a `NUM_WORKERS` variable to the bash script's input variables. This will allow users to set the number of workers according to their needs.

Here is how you can modify the `run_infer.sh` scripts to include the `NUM_WORKERS` variable:

1. **Add `NUM_WORKERS` as an input variable.**
2. **Set a default value for `NUM_WORKERS` if it is not provided.**
3. **Update the command to use the `NUM_WORKERS` variable.**

Below is an example of how you can modify one of the scripts (`evaluation/toolqa/scripts/run_infer.sh`). You can apply similar changes to the other scripts.

### Modified `evaluation/toolqa/scripts/run_infer.sh`

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -eo pipefail

source "evaluation/utils/version_control.sh"

MODEL_CONFIG=$1
COMMIT_HASH=$2
AGENT=$3
EVAL_LIMIT=$4
DATASET=$5
HARDNESS=$6
WOLFRAM_APPID=$7
NUM_WORKERS=${8:-1}  # Add NUM_WORKERS variable with default value 1

checkout_eval_branch

if [ -z "$AGENT" ]; then
  echo "Agent not specified, use default CodeActAgent"
  AGENT="CodeActAgent"
fi

if [ -z "$DATASET" ]; then
  DATASET="flight"
  echo "Dataset not specified, use default $DATASET"
fi

if [ -z "$HARDNESS" ]; then
  HARDNESS="easy"
  echo "Hardness not specified, use default $HARDNESS"
fi

if [ -z "$WOLFRAM_APPID" ]; then
  WOLFRAM_APPID="YOUR_WOLFRAMALPHA_APPID"
  echo "WOLFRAM_APPID not specified"
fi

get_agent_version

echo "AGENT: $AGENT"
echo "AGENT_VERSION: $AGENT_VERSION"
echo "MODEL_CONFIG: $MODEL_CONFIG"
echo "DATASET: $DATASET"
echo "HARDNESS: $HARDNESS"
echo "WOLFRAM_APPID: $WOLFRAM_APPID"
echo "NUM_WORKERS: $NUM_WORKERS"  # Print NUM_WORKERS

COMMAND="poetry run python evaluation/toolqa/run_infer.py \
  --agent-cls $AGENT \
  --llm-config $MODEL_CONFIG \
  --max-iterations 30 \
  --dataset $DATASET \
  --hardness $HARDNESS \
  --wolfram_alpha_appid $WOLFRAM_APPID \
  --data-split validation \
  --max-chars 10000000 \
  --eval-num-workers $NUM_WORKERS \  # Use NUM_WORKERS variable
  --eval-note ${AGENT_VERSION}_${LEVELS}"

if [ -n "$EVAL_LIMIT" ]; then
  echo "EVAL_LIMIT: $EVAL_LIMIT"
  COMMAND="$COMMAND --eval-n-limit $EVAL_LIMIT"
fi

# Run the command
eval $COMMAND
```

### Apply Similar Changes to Other Scripts

You can apply similar changes to the other `run_infer.sh` scripts in the `evaluation` directory. Here is a summary of the changes:

1. Add `NUM_WORKERS=${8:-1}` to the list of input variables.
2. Print the `NUM_WORKERS` variable for debugging purposes.
3. Update the `COMMAND` to use the `--eval-num-workers $NUM_WORKERS` option.

By making these changes, users will be able to specify the number of workers when running the scripts, providing greater flexibility and consistency across different evaluation benchmarks.

body:
Here are my installation steps. They are a bit different from the ones in the documentation and might help you:

1. Install Poetry and Node.js
2. In the project, run `poetry install` (or use PyCharm to set up a virtual environment with Poetry)
3. Run `make setup-config` to generate the configuration file
4. Go to the frontend folder and run `npm run make-18n` and then run `npm run build`
5. Go back to the opendevin root directory and run `make start-backend` to start the backend project
6. Go back to the frontend directory and run `npm run start` to start the frontend project

After this, you should be able to visit the opendevin website. You might encounter some docker issues, but you can follow the documentation to resolve them.

body:
The error message indicates that Docker is unable to start the container because the path `/tmp/cache` is not shared from the host and is not known to Docker. This is a common issue when Docker is not configured to share certain directories with containers.

Here are the steps to resolve this issue:

1. **Configure Docker to Share the Path**:
   - Open Docker Desktop.
   - Go to `Preferences` (or `Settings` on Windows).
   - Navigate to `Resources` -> `File Sharing`.
   - Add `/tmp/cache` to the list of shared paths.
   - Apply and restart Docker.

2. **Verify Docker Configuration**:
   Ensure that Docker is running and properly configured to share the necessary paths. You can verify this by running:
   ```bash
   docker info
   ```
   and checking the `File Descriptors` section to see if the paths are correctly shared.

3. **Check Docker Version**:
   Make sure you are using a compatible version of Docker. Sometimes, upgrading Docker to the latest version can resolve such issues.

4. **Update Docker Configuration in Code**:
   If the path `/tmp/cache` is hardcoded in your code, consider making it configurable. This can be done by updating the configuration files or environment variables used in your Docker setup.

5. **Refer to Docker Documentation**:
   For more details on configuring shared paths, refer to the Docker documentation: [Docker File Sharing](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/mac/#file-sharing).

6. **Check the Troubleshooting Guide**:
   The repository includes a troubleshooting guide that might have additional information on resolving Docker-related issues. You can find it in `/docs/modules/usage/troubleshooting/troubleshooting.md`.

By following these steps, you should be able to resolve the issue with Docker not being able to start the container due to the unshared path. If the problem persists, consider checking the Docker logs for more detailed error messages and further debugging.

body:
Edit: Got it working with these steps.

1. Find the `podman.sock` location
```zsh
podman info --format "{{.Host.RemoteSocket.Path}}"
/run/user/502/podman/podman.sock
```
2. Set permissions on `podman.sock` inside the podman machine 
```zsh
podman machine ssh
Connecting to vm podman-machine-default. To close connection, use `~.` or `exit`
Fedora CoreOS 39.20240407.2.0
Tracker: https://github.com/coreos/fedora-coreos-tracker
Discuss: https://discussion.fedoraproject.org/tag/coreos

Last login: Fri Aug 16 19:18:33 2024 from 192.168.127.1
core@localhost:~$ sudo chmod 666 /run/user/502/podman/podman.sock
core@localhost:~$ exit
logout
```
3. Launch the container
```zsh
export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/502/podman/podman.sock

WORKSPACE_BASE=$(pwd)/workspace
docker run -it \
    --pull=always \
    --privileged \
    -e SANDBOX_USER_ID=$(id -u) \
    -e WORKSPACE_MOUNT_PATH=$WORKSPACE_BASE \
    -v $WORKSPACE_BASE:/opt/workspace_base:z \
    -v /run/user/502/podman/podman.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:Z \
    -p 3005:3000 \
    --name opendevin-app-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S) \
    ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin:0.8
```
    
 
## Original comment
I get an `stat: cannot statx '/var/run/docker.sock': Permission denied` error trying to use the following command with Podman installed on macOS (docker is aliased to podman).
```

body:
### Below is a suggestion for rewording the Getting Started section of the README file.

The easiest way to run OpenDevin is inside a Docker container by following these steps. Adjust as needed for your particular needs.
- Create an environment variable to tell the container where on the host machine to store files. As the container runs, the files in this workspace may be modified or deleted.
```
export WORKSPACE_BASE=$(pwd)/workspace
```
- If you'd like, you can create an environment variable to tell the container the API key for OpenAI. Another approach is to click the gear at the bottom right of the web page after the container is running. Without using one of these options, OpenDevin will encounter errors as it attempts to respond to user prompts.
```
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-XXXXX
```
- Run the docker container. This particular command runs the container in interactive mode. This means you'll see STDOUT mesages scroll by as the container initializes and runs. When you see a  line that contains "Uvicorn running" then the container is ready. Stop the container by using ctrl-c. This will stop and remove the container. As of 2024-07-01, make sure to specify the "0.7" version because the "latest" tag is an older version. Optionally add "-e OPENAI_API_KEY=$OPENAI_API_KEY \" if you want to pass the OpenAI API key to the container.
```shell
docker run -it \
    --rm \
    --pull=always \
    -e SANDBOX_USER_ID=$(id -u) \
    -e WORKSPACE_MOUNT_PATH=$WORKSPACE_BASE \
    -v $WORKSPACE_BASE:/opt/workspace_base \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -p 3000:3000 \
    --add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
    --name opendevin \
    ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin:0.7
```
- Visit [http://0.0.0.0:3000](http://0.0.0.0:3000/) to see OpenDevin in action. OpenDevin will only have access to the  workspace folder on the host machine. The rest of your system will not be affected as it runs in a secure docker sandbox.
- Until you learn more, leave the CodeActAgent Agent selected in the configuration settings.
If you are ready to run OpenDevin all the time (in the background), use the following version of the docker command:
```
docker run -d \
    --pull=always \
    -e SANDBOX_USER_ID=$(id -u) \
    -e OPENAI_API_KEY=$OPENAI_API_KEY \
    -e WORKSPACE_MOUNT_PATH=$WORKSPACE_BASE \
    -v $WORKSPACE_BASE:/opt/workspace_base \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -p 3000:3000 \
    --add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
    --name OpenDevin \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin:0.7
```
As needed, you can see the STDOUT of the container using this command. Press ctrl-c when you want to stop viewing the logs.
```
docker logs -f OpenDevin
```

Just to get you started, here are a sequence of instructors to create a simple python script and unit tests.
 - Create a module for some basic functionality.
```
create a python module that serves as a number generator. As needed, i will pass start and end numbers. Then I want to iterate over the range of the two numbers.
```
- Create and run unit tests.
```
now create a comprehensive suite of unit tests that can be run using pytest.
```
- Run pylint to perform static code analysis and fix any issues found.
```
lastly, run pylint and fix any issues that it finds.
```

though the solution seems straightforward here, we need to add the latest tag, we can do so like `tags+=("latest")`

however, we should decide when to apply 'latest' on all builds or only when building a release version e.g (0.7.0)
```

if [[ -n $GITHUB_REF_NAME ]]; then
  # check if ref name is a version number
  if [[ $GITHUB_REF_NAME =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    major_version=$(echo "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" | cut -d. -f1)
    minor_version=$(echo "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" | cut -d. -f1,2)
    tags+=("$major_version" "$minor_version")
    
    tags+=("latest")  # This will add latest only when we build for stable version numbers
    
  fi
  sanitized=$(echo "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" | sed 's/[^a-zA-Z0-9.-]\+/-/g')
  OPEN_DEVIN_BUILD_VERSION=$sanitized
  tag=$(echo "$sanitized" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]') # lower case is required in tagging
  tags+=("$tag")
  
  tags+=("latest")  # This will add latest every time we build a new container.  
   
fi
```
Your thoughts on this?

I'm using ast to read the python files. And astor to write the python code with the placeholder docstrings. I've found a bug in astor. It can't correctly parse the following docstring. 

```
        """
            \x00
        """
```

Now I'm curious. Is there some C code somewhere reading the \x00 as an end-of-string? 

astor prints that comment as

```
'\n            \x00\n        '
```
author: medined

body:
With the help of this bash command I tried to find any .py file with that character _not_ being the end-of-file character:
`find . -name '*.py' -type f -print0 | xargs -0 grep -Pzl '\x00(?!.*\x00\z)'`
Could you run that in your OpenDevin folder, please, and report if any files were found?
author: tobitege

body:
That command finds no files. The file (or one of them) causing issues with astor is opendevin/runtime/docker/process.py. It's the existing docstring for parser_docker_exec_output.

P.S. Thanks for indulging my eccentricity on this topic.
author: medined

body:
No worries 😀 

Edit: nvm, just read the comment fully lol
author: tobitege

body:
Ohhhh lol...
that docstring has: `>> b'\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x13Hello OpenDevin!'`
But that is plain ASCII, not binary... 🤣 

I'm sorry, I should've read your above post more closely, I was reading it as if it found the actual hex value 0 somehow.
So it does seem an issue with astor, I'd agree. @medined
author: tobitege

body: Sadly, I have verified that changing the existing docstring to \\x00 avoids the issue. And, of course, it makes no sense to alter the original comment to use \\x00 - that looks stupid. If anyone wants to follow the excitement over on the astor project, the issue is at https://github.com/berkerpeksag/astor/issues/225.

Could you manually run the following command in the sandbox by connecting via SSH as per the steps provided in the log?

```
git diff --no-color --cached b16c7d12ccbc7b2d20364b89fb44285bcbfede54
```

Git will give paginated output if the diff is large enough. This can be disabled with the `--no-pager` option. Could you check if that's the case?
author: SmartManoj

body: Thanks, this is exactly the reason,  the `ssh.prompt` will try to look for the `# (root user) or $ (other user)`. The `pager` setting will block it.  I added a new line : `exit_code, output = self.execute('git config --global core.pager ""')` before executing `git add -A`. I think it should be good now. Just submitted a PR # https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2828.  Thanks!

```
-e OPENAI_API_KEY=anything
-e CUSTOM_LLM_PROVIDER=openai

Please find "Example Usage" in the documentation by litellm for custom api server:
https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/custom_openai_proxy

body:
> > Instead of ACR, how about implementing 'mentat auto context'.
> 
> This issue aims to provide the agent with tools more tailored for coding tasks, improving upon the available search tools OpenDevin already has (using it or not depends on the agent). Mentat's auto context, if I understand correctly, is a way to automatically append the retrieved code snippets for the last user message into the prompt before sending to the LLM. This may be a useful feature we want to incorporate and try out for normal agent usage (I can have a closer look into the implementation), but I'm afraid it may not always help for the swe-bench evaluation of the agent:
> 
> * The retrieved code may not be useful for the issue, which negatively affect how the agent behaves accordingly (similarly to how the score decreases [Add Aider-inspired RepoMap #2248](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2248))
> * Their `MentatBot` use another approach, not this one, is that correct? (something called `Library Context`)
> 
> > Also, correct me if I'm wrong. Doesn't it serve the same purpose of pr #2518?
> 
> They are both to enhance code searching ability I think, just in different approaches.

both auto-context and library context in Mentat are designed to draw relevant context specific to the project and issues at hand. However, they do so in slightly different ways:

Auto-context automatically selects relevant code snippets up to a preset token limit (e.g., 5000 tokens) to provide a broad, dynamically generated context. This feature uses embeddings to identify and include code snippets that are most pertinent to the user's current task, which might span across the entire codebase. It's especially useful for tasks that require a general understanding of various parts of the project but don't have predefined specific targets.

Library context, used by tools like Mentat Bot, is more targeted. It specifically draws on detailed documentation and project issues to guide the coding tasks, such as generating pull requests or resolving issues. This approach is structured to pull in context that is directly relevant to the task defined by project documentation or GitHub issues, making it ideal for precise and specific coding tasks.

While both methods aim to integrate relevant information, auto-context is more about breadth and adaptability, whereas library context focuses on the depth and specificity of the task derived from documentation and issue details.

in other words, they are both relatively the same with slight modifications where auto-context is more similar to 'repomap' and library context to ACR's approach primary difference being vector db. maybe a hybrid of repomap, auto-context, and ACR's context search API with switch statements can tackle both use cases more effectively.

> > I believe it's a similar process as 'anythingLLM' where you can load a whole github repo to knowledge-base under a minute.
> 
> Like this RepoMap #2248?

Sounds similar, but is quite different, let Sonnet explain why:
`This Python code implements a system for analyzing and mapping a code repository, which is fundamentally different from using a vector database. Let me explain the key differences and what this code does:

1. Repository Analysis:
   This code analyzes the structure and content of a code repository by parsing source files, extracting information about defined and referenced identifiers (like function names, class names, etc.), and building a graph-based representation of the codebase.

2. Tag Extraction:
   It uses tree-sitter and Pygments to parse source code files and extract "tags" - which are essentially identifiers and their locations in the code. These tags are cached for performance.

3. Graph-based Ranking:
   The code builds a graph where nodes are files and edges represent relationships between files based on shared identifiers. It then uses PageRank algorithm to rank the importance of files and identifiers in the codebase.

4. Context-aware Mapping:
   The system generates a "map" of the repository that focuses on the most relevant parts of the codebase, taking into account which files are currently being discussed (chat_files) and which identifiers have been mentioned.

5. Token-based Sizing:
   The code aims to create a repository map that fits within a specified token limit, which is likely for use with a language model like GPT.

In contrast, a vector database approach would typically work as follows:

1. Embedding Generation:
   Each file or code snippet would be converted into a high-dimensional vector representation (embedding) using a model trained on code.

2. Similarity Search:
   When querying the codebase, you would convert the query into a vector and find the most similar vectors in the database.

3. Retrieval:
   The most relevant code snippets or files would be retrieved based on vector similarity.

Key differences:

1. Structural Understanding: 
   This code has a deeper structural understanding of the codebase, including relationships between files and identifiers. A vector database typically doesn't capture these relationships explicitly.

2. Ranking Method:
   This code uses graph-based ranking, while vector databases use vector similarity.

3. Context Awareness:
   This system can adjust its representation based on the current context of the conversation. Vector databases typically don't have this level of dynamic adjustment.

4. Token Economy:
   This system is designed to work within token limits, which is not typically a concern for vector databases.

5. Language-specific Analysis:
   This code uses language-specific parsers to understand code structure. Vector databases often use more general text-based approaches.

In summary, this code provides a more detailed, structure-aware, and context-sensitive analysis of a codebase, tailored for use with language models, compared to the simpler but potentially more scalable approach of vector databases.`

Note: instead of making a embedding of a segment of code, it would be better to make an embedding of a **summary** of that segment of code. That way the semantic meaning captured in the embedding would be more relevant to that segment of code versus making an embedding of the code itself. **K-nearest-matching embeddings should lead to nodes on the graph, and then retrieval should rely on subgraph traversal.**

I asked to chatgpt but I know that people often do not like when we use AI Assistants to help with code 😏 so yeah I have no idea if this is relevant to anything at all:



The issue in the code located at [OpenDevin/opendevin/runtime/server/files.py](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/9b0ff117abd176a4a75233dc65819c0f13ad5c00/opendevin/runtime/server/files.py#L90) is that the `content` variable is being split using the `split('\n')` method, which expects `content` to be a string. If `content` is a dictionary, this will cause the `AttributeError`.

Script used to clean all containers & volumes : 

```sh
#!/bin/bash

set -e

CONTAINERS=$(docker ps -aq --filter "name=opendevin")
VOLUMES=$(docker volume ls -q --filter "name=opendevin")

CONTAINERS_COUNT=$(echo "$CONTAINERS" | wc -w)
VOLUMES_COUNT=$(echo "$VOLUMES" | wc -w)

echo "Found $CONTAINERS_COUNT containers and $VOLUMES_COUNT volumes containing 'opendevin'"

if [ -n "$CONTAINERS" ]; then
  docker rm -f $CONTAINERS
  echo "Removed $CONTAINERS_COUNT containers"
fi

if docker image inspect ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin:latest &>/dev/null; then
  echo "Image found, removing..."
  docker rmi ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin:latest
else
  echo "Image not found, skipping removal"
fi

docker builder prune -af

if [ -n "$VOLUMES" ]; then
  docker volume rm $VOLUMES
  echo "Removed $VOLUMES_COUNT volumes"
fi

echo "Done"
```

Could you run this to check whether the API is working properly?
```python
from litellm import completion
from datetime import datetime
import os

if os.path.exists('config.toml'):
    from toml import load
    config = load('config.toml')
else:
    config = {
        'LLM_MODEL': 'ollama/llama3',
        'LLM_API_KEY': None,
        'LLM_BASE_URL': None
    }

messages = [{ "content": "If there are 10 books in a room and I read 2, how many books are still in the room?","role": "user"}]
dt = datetime.now()
response = completion(model=config['LLM_MODEL'], 
                        api_key=config['LLM_API_KEY'],
                        base_url=config['LLM_BASE_URL'],
                      messages=messages)

content = response.choices[0].message.content
print(content)

if '8' in content:
    print('--> Correct answer! 🎉')
    print('There are still 10 books in the room; reading them does not reduce the count. Consider exploring more accurate models for better results.')

dt2 = datetime.now()
print('Used model:',config['LLM_MODEL'])
print(f"Time taken: {(dt2-dt).total_seconds():.1f}s")
```

                        api_key=config['LLM_API_KEY'],
                        base_url=config['LLM_BASE_URL'],
                        api_version=config['LLM_API_VERSION'],
                      messages=messages)

content = response.choices[0].message.content
print(content)

if '8' in content:
    print('--> Correct answer! 🎉')
    print('There are still 10 books in the room; reading them does not reduce the count. Consider exploring more accurate models for better results.')

dt2 = datetime.now()
print('Used model:',config['LLM_MODEL'])
print(f"Time taken: {(dt2-dt).total_seconds():.1f}s")
```

body:
First, great collection of issues to look into!

> Fixes
>  ...if we've been waiting for more than 5s...

As to that 2nd point: if the model runs any installations (like with pip), these 5 seconds could become too short?

> Add something in the prompt...

We may have to track down the "usual suspects" IF these have parameters especially to suppress interactive mode:
Several package installers have parameters to suppress interactive mode. Here are the options for some of the most common ones (thx to Sonnet):

1. **pip**:
   - Use the `-q` or `--quiet` flag to suppress output.
   - Use the `-y` or `--yes` flag to automatically answer yes to prompts (though `pip` itself doesn't typically prompt for yes/no).

   ```bash
   pip install -q package_name
   ```

2. **Poetry**:
   - Poetry does not have interactive prompts during installation, so no specific flag is needed to suppress them.

3. **npm**:
   - Use the `--yes` or `-y` flag to automatically answer yes to prompts.

   ```bash
   npm install package_name --yes
   ```

4. **yarn**:
   - Yarn does not typically have interactive prompts during installation, so no specific flag is needed to suppress them.

5. **conda**:
   - Use the `-y` or `--yes` flag to automatically answer yes to prompts.

   ```bash
   conda install package_name -y
   ```

6. **apt-get** (for system packages on Debian-based systems):
   - Use the `-y` or `--yes` flag to automatically answer yes to prompts.

   ```bash
   sudo apt-get install package_name -y
   ```
author: tobitege

body:
> if the model runs any installations (like with pip), these 5 seconds could become too short?

Yeah.. that's a good point and that's primarily why we did implement the timeout but not this.

I guess the `T` second timeout should be enforced for the stream of output: e.g., if the terminal keeps printing outputs in the last `T` second duration (e.g., you see the screen rolling when running installation command), then it is probably working fine without interactions. But if it hangs for `T` second (no output is printing), then it probably needs someone to look to see if we need to enter/do anything.

I mean, we humans do the same thing! If a command hangs unreasonably long, we might just issue `ctrl+C` to kill it 😅 

Maybe we could (1) switch everything to streaming outputs, (2) just wait for `T=10` seconds, (3) if no additional outputs are added during that last `T` seconds, we are probably stuck - we can let the LLM decide whether it wants to (a) interrupt the process, (b) enter something if this is actually a legit interactive prompt, (c) keep waiting. IMO this might be the next level of *agents* that is execution time aware 😆

body:
> Big picture view for me is this (just speaking for myself): models aren't as capable as we wished they were, and might not be for some while. I think I replied similarly in a different issue of yours, so I won't repeat myself here. 😁


I understand we haven't reached the AGI yet but that's not the point.

developer agents have reached up to 43% on swe-bench eval when the model powering those agents can only get up to 2-5% with RAG. Prompt engineering has also been shown to extract way more from models than regular prompting. This proves the capabilities of a model aren't limited to itself but up to the usage (agents and effective prompting).

Evals are relatively isolated issues compared to issues from real-world projects. real projects have various aspects that need to be kept in mind while generating code for it to be usable. projects are very diverse and dynamic simply because the same function can be written in almost infinite ways depending on the programmer though some uniformity is advised also 2 same project can be stacked with completely different tools and libraries despite achieving the same goal. 

My point is in real usage, agents need to account for various things besides just the code snippets for it to be functional with the rest of the projects, and with each project, it will be different. Due to overfitting, you can make an LLM score almost 100 on any eval but that comes with a huge price which is losing its generalizing capabilities and not being able to function correctly when faced with previously unseen data. 

working on a real issue doesn't mean creating something that hasn't been done before instead most of the time it's something that has been implemented in multiple places with slight modifications due to the relevant source code of that project. developing agents with the goal of excelling on eval makes it overfitted to perform well on isolated issues which is great if it's used to create a single Python script. however, real projects have various aspects from dependencies to existing source code so even when given a task to generate a simple code snippet, that needs to be compatible with all that already exists within the project and that's something that won't be developed properly if it's only tested with isolated interview questions (evals). 

it's the same reason college exam papers don't reflect real-world problems. just like experience is more valuable than a degree, developing the agents against real issues is more valuable than an eval score. 

Also when agents are used by the developers like how the ideal version should/will be used by users, it will be easier for them to figure out what are the features missing and how to actually overcome the current limitations. 

I know the industry isn't "there" yet but the approach we take will decide when we get there or if we even get there or not. I hope I was able to make my point clear and I'm sorry for my ignorance as I'm still learning in this rapidly growing field.

I don't think anyone is disagreeing with you at all :). Your points are valid and make sense.
All I'm saying is this particular issue is not actionable. It is more suited as a discussion with people. You can say "Make OpenDevin Better" and although that is valid ask, it is not actionable.

I think it's actionable to create issues for OD to solve as well as use it on local tasks to test its limitations. With each failure/success, we can understand better what's causing the problem and how that can be overcome. 

At least once a week, if it's tested in a real environment, upon inspecting the outcome, a lot can be learned. 

Required skills needed to keep a whole project in context while generating code won't be properly developed if it's only tested on isolated issues (evals). However, you guys are the experts, so i trust your judgment. I wish at least once it's properly discussed among the team, including the discussion #2936

body:
`PERSIST_SANDBOX` config will do that.
```
WORKSPACE_BASE=$(pwd)/workspace
docker run -it \
    --pull=always \
    -e PERSIST_SANDBOX=true \
    -e SANDBOX_USER_ID=$(id -u) \
    -e WORKSPACE_MOUNT_PATH=$WORKSPACE_BASE \
    -v $WORKSPACE_BASE:/opt/workspace_base \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -p 3000:3000 \
    --add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
    --name opendevin-app-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S) \
    ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin
```

or you can use a [Custom Docker Sandbox](https://docs.all-hands.dev/modules/usage/custom_sandbox_guide).
author: SmartManoj

body:
Hello! Between the time that the packages need to be installed, does OpenDevin restart? If it does, that would explain it.
OpenDevin uses a sandbox which is a docker container and that's where it installs all the packages. If OpenDevin restarts, then that sandbox gets deleted and you lose your installed packages.

If you want the same packages installed all the time, you could follow this guide to create a docker image and use it as a starting image for OpenDevin: https://docs.all-hands.dev/modules/usage/custom_sandbox_guide
This is the recommended way.

You could also set `PERSIST_SANDBOX=true` as suggested above, but that may be a bit buggy depending on what you do.

Easy as pie. I'm a FreeBSD guy, so my Docker-fu is very weak and I don't really use Ollama, but with LocalAI, it is a cinch. Normally, I run the build version but tried this on an Ubuntu 22 LTS, a fresh Mint and just firing it up on Debian:

Grab LocalAI via the bash installer if you really want easy:

```bash
curl https://localai.io/install.sh | sh
```

You can specify options while grabbing, but if you don't, the script will try to do the right thing (ie, if you have Docker and CUDA runtime container toolkit, it'll go that route)

Fair warning, the image is pretty large, cuz it has a lot pre-baked in (tts, stt, text to image gen, etc etc). As far as I know, LocalAI was the first and only opensource project to maintain feature parity with OpenAI API nearly from the beginning, while it seems others are bolting on and starting to catch up, LocalAI is maturing on all fronts and even has a simple and elegant web-ui for browsing models, quick prompt/inference testing, etc.

Or, you could download the binary from the Github. Or, if you are a very high level Warlock, you could attempt to build from source, but be warned, many submodules make it sometimes tricky!

At any rate, once the script is finished, it will tell you LocalAI is up and running on *:8080, if you didn't change it.

Now, what I usually do is have LiteLLM proxy running:
```bash
 litellm --model openai/gpt-3.5-turbo --host 0.0.0.0 --port 11434 --api_base 'http://10.10.10.10:8080/v1' --detailed_debug --alias synthia34b-awq
 ```
 
 That way, I can swap llm's out underneath whatever app(s) on whichever boxen.
 
 But you could do an ssh -L proxy if you need to work around docker host internal networking issues:
 
 ```bash
  ssh -L 0.0.0.0:11434:192.168.50.65:8080 localhost -N     
  ```
  
  Here's an OpenDevin startup that will have you right as rain:
  
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash

export OPENAI_API_BASE=http://192.168.50.41:8080/v1
export WORKSPACE_BASE=/home/matto/workspace

docker run \
    -it \
    --add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
    -e SANDBOX_USER_ID="opendevin" \
    -e LLM_API_KEY="stfu" \
    -e LLM_MODEL="openai/gpt-3.5-turbo" \
    -e LLM_BASE_URL="http://172.18.0.1:11434" \
    -e WORKSPACE_MOUNT_PATH=$WORKSPACE_BASE \
    -v $WORKSPACE_BASE:/opt/workspace_base \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -p 3000:3000 \
    ghcr.io/opendevin/opendevin:latest
  
# Plus whatever else you crazy Docker kids do!
    ##--pull=always 
    #-e SANDBOX_USER_ID=$(id -u) 
```
    
FYI: I'm sure I am doing it wrong, but when wrong works right, I'm ok with it. 
Just tried OpenDevin out this last weekend and wow, what a fantastic project! Thanks for open-sourcing and keep up the killer work.

I'll see about getting some of my MemGPT prompts going in here and post if I find anything interesting :D

Sorry to hear that! How many processes you are using (`N_PROCESS`)? Maybe you can try to tune that down to 1 to see if the issue persists?

Here's the pointer i got from claude sonnet 3.5:

> This error suggests that the Docker daemon is not responding within the expected time frame (60 seconds). This could be due to several reasons:
> The Docker daemon is overloaded or not responding properly.
> There might be network issues if Docker is running on a remote machine.
> The system running Docker might be under heavy load, causing slow responses.
> There could be a large number of containers or images, causing the listing operation to take too long.

You could also try check how many containers are running in your system `docker ps` -- if there's too many stale containers, you can try to stop them first to free up system resources (e.g., `docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep opendevin | xargs docker stop`)

BTW, we are working on a new Runtime for eval (#2404) that completely gets rid of the SSHBox that can sometimes be unstable in the coming weeks - Hopefully this can work better for these evals.
